verdicts.trueWording: When I switch to another character's point of view, the conversation isn't the same. It bears a resemblance, but it's not the same.
verdicts.note: LARB raw HTML fetched 200 via curl with a browser UA; quote is verbatim in the answer on multiple points of view. Both limbs (resemblance, not the same) explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: if a reader can pick out what's made up and what's real, you've botched your storytelling!
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the LARB raw page, in the answer following the Hilary Mantel / interrogating-a-version-of-the-past question. Page adds an exclamation mark; wording otherwise identical.

verdicts.trueWording: That's also one of the reasons I've used two moons in several of the books. The two moons say, We're not here.
verdicts.note: Verbatim on LARB raw page. The 'as a signal' limb is supported by the question it answers ('you're setting the rules of engagement? So your reader knows you're not talking about Justinian himself?' — 'That's right.').

verdicts.trueWording: Any strength for the writer, from form, from craft, from technique, becomes a strength for the reader, because we're in this together.
verdicts.note: Verbatim on LARB raw page, in the final substantive answer of the interview, exactly as the page label 'closing answer' says.

verdicts.trueWording: The reading I was doing brought home to me that the ambitions and doings of emperors and empresses and sultans and dukes of powerful city-states didn't really matter that much to the day-to-day desires and ambitions and needs of ordinary people living on the borderlands.
verdicts.note: Verbatim on LARB raw page, in the answer to the follow-up about honouring the legacies of fathers. Every limb (his reading, emperors and sultans, day-to-day needs, borderlands) explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't write any 'one to one' allegories. I'm not writing books about the past that I mean to have the reader feel that's exactly what's happening now.
verdicts.note: CBC raw HTML fetched 200; both sentences verbatim, in the answer to 'Do you feel you need to pay attention to what's happening in the world when you write?'

verdicts.trueWording: When I talk about process and method I always preface it to say this is anecdotal, not prescriptive.
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the CBC raw page, in the answer to 'What is your approach to storytelling? Do you outline first?' Claim's 'prefaces it by saying' vs page's 'preface it to say' is the same sentence; the quoted span itself is word for word.

verdicts.trueWording: Shirley Hazzard's The Transit of Venus. I don't write like that, but my admiration for the craft and intelligence, the sentence by sentence insight and brilliance is extreme.
verdicts.note: Lit Hub raw HTML fetched 200; verbatim in the answer to 'Is there a book you wish you had written?' Both limbs (does not write like that; admiration extreme) explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: One of the things I'm really interested in is memory. We make stories of our lives and we remember the same moments differently.
verdicts.note: Locus 'Journeying' raw HTML fetched 200; verbatim in the final excerpt (page carries soft hyphens inside 'really', which do not render). Both limbs explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: I did this very deliberately, five or six times I think, to underscore the way in which we remember and hear and respond differently to the same moments.
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Locus 'Journeying' final excerpt. 'this book' is Children of Earth and Sky, named on the same page in the preceding excerpt and in the bio; the technique described is the mid-conversation POV cut with repeated, slightly altered dialogue.

verdicts.trueWording: My proofreader, quite correctly, flagged every one of these as an error ... What I prefer is the change! The difference.
verdicts.note: Both limbs verbatim in the Locus 'Journeying' final excerpt, adjacent sentences. Kay adds 'quite correctly' and gives the proofreader's query in full.

verdicts.trueWording: It's a wonderful passage about how the concerns of ordinary people are not those that we tend to see if we read the overarching histories of a given time ... None of these are important people.
verdicts.note: Both limbs on the Locus 'Journeying' third excerpt, which names Fernand Braudel as the source of the passage. The number five is a count of the page's own enumeration — the one caught up in the war plus an artist, a woman escaping her father's plan, a merchant and a soldier — immediately followed by 'None of these are important people'; the page does not print the word 'five' or the word 'protagonists'.

verdicts.trueWording: It's fun writing a bad writer, too. I did a bad troubadour early in A Song for Arbonne, and it's ridiculously enjoyable to hack around with a hack's work.
verdicts.note: Locus 'Margins of History' raw HTML fetched 200; verbatim in the excerpt about the poets of Written on the Dark (Marina di Seressa and Thierry Villar), immediately after 'There are a couple of other poets in the novel.'

verdicts.trueWording: I think every serious writer is teaching a reader how to read them. That fits into a classic paradigm: If you think someone's poured you a cup of coffee, but they've poured you tea, your first sip is, 'Oh!'
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Locus 'Margins of History' excerpt; the coffee/tea limb is the sentence directly following, so both limbs are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't ever want to write a book where things map directly - where a character maps onto a real person, or where an event maps precisely onto a real event.
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Locus 'Margins of History' excerpt, in the paragraph on 'History doesn't repeat, but it rhymes'. All three limbs explicit.
